### Motivation

In order to define continuity of funtions, we need to define limits in the context of functions. Previously, we defined the limit of a sequence. Given a function $f:S\to\mathbb{R}$, this allows us to see how $f(x)$ behaves as $x$ tends to a certain point.

### Cluster points

The cluster points of a set $S\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ are the points $x\in\mathbb{R}$ that have elements of $S$ aribitrarily near. Equivalently, $x$ is a cluster point of $S$ if $\forall \varepsilon >0$, the neighborhood $(x-\varepsilon, x+\varepsilon)$ contains infinitely many elements of $S$. 

However, since epsilon can take any arbitraily small value, demonstrating that there exists an element of $S$ in $(x-\varepsilon, x+\varepsilon)\setminus\{x\}$ is sufficient. Consider if there were only finite many elements of $S$ in the $\varepsilon$-neighborhood of $x$. Then, we could always choose an epsilon small enough such that the neighborhood contains none of the elements of $S$ except possibly $x$, which is excluded in $(x-\varepsilon, x+\varepsilon)\setminus\{x\}$.

::: {#def-cluster-point}
Given a set $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}$, a number
$x\in\mathbb{R}$ is called a **cluster point**
of $S$ if, for every $\varepsilon>0$,

$$
((x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\setminus\{x\})
\cap S\neq\varnothing.
$$
:::

Notice that a cluster point of $S$ may not be an element of $S$ itself.
